\chapter{Five More Short Answers --- Maybe, Could Be, Indeed, No Doubt, Out of the Question}
\label{ch:mas-respuestas}
\hlchaptermodality{298}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer someone in Spanish anywhere from maybe to out of the question, and say how strong each answer is.}

Complete ES-C298-ni-hablar: give all five answers in order, from the weakest to the flattest.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tal vez]{tal vez — such a turn}

\label{lesson:ES-C298-tal-vez}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what was \emph{allium}? (Garlic.) And did \emph{suppa} mean the bread or the broth? (The bread.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item quizás — the other way to say this, which you already have.
  \item de acuerdo — the answer at the opposite end.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tal VEZ}, with the weight on the second word. The \emph{v} is a \emph{b}, and the \emph{z} is a plain \emph{s} in most of the Spanish-speaking world. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tal vez} — \textquotedblleft{}maybe,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}perhaps.\textquotedblright{}

Two pieces. \emph{Tal} means \textquotedblleft{}such,\textquotedblright{} and \emph{vez} is Latin \textbf{vicem}: a turn, a going round, one occasion out of several. So \emph{tal vez} is \textquotedblleft{}such a turn\textquotedblright{} — this time it might fall this way, another time it might not.

\emph{Vicem} is generous to English. \textbf{Vice versa} is \textquotedblleft{}the turn having been turned.\textquotedblright{} A \textbf{vicar} stands in someone's turn, and so does a \textbf{vice-president}. \textbf{Vicissitude} is life doing the turning without asking you.

You already have \emph{quizás} for the same job. The difference is small but real: \emph{quizás} leans on not knowing, and \emph{tal vez} leans on it happening to fall out that way. Either answers a question you cannot answer.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five answers, and the least committed of them.

The run ahead is a dial. It starts here, at \textquotedblleft{}possibly,\textquotedblright{} and ends somewhere you would not want to point at a stranger.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tal vez}
  \item \emph{quizás}, then \emph{tal vez}
  \item \emph{tal vez mañana}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{vicem} mean? (A turn, an occasion.) What is \emph{vice versa}, taken literally? (The turn turned round.) And what does \emph{tal vez} answer? (Maybe.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puede ser]{puede ser — nothing new in it}

\label{lesson:ES-C298-puede-ser}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what did \emph{suppa} mean? (The soaked bread.) And what does \emph{vicem} mean inside \emph{tal vez}? (A turn, an occasion.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item poder — the first half.
  \item ser — the second.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PUE-de SER}, two beats then one. The \emph{ue} is a single slide, not two steps. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{puede ser} — \textquotedblleft{}could be,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}it may be so.\textquotedblright{}

There is nothing here you do not already own. \emph{Poder}, to be able, with its stressed \emph{o} cracking open into \emph{ue} the way it always does. \emph{Ser}, to be. Put them together and you have said \textquotedblleft{}it is able to be,\textquotedblright{} which is a very exact description of what \textquotedblleft{}maybe\textquotedblright{} actually claims.

That is worth noticing on its own. Some of the most useful things you can say in a language are not new material at all — they are two familiar pieces standing in the right order, and the only thing you were missing was permission to put them there.

Against \emph{tal vez}, this one is warmer. \emph{Tal vez} is a shrug at the odds. \emph{Puede ser} concedes that the other person might be right, which is why it so often comes just before somebody changes their mind.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two answers, and a way of getting more of them free.

Every time you learn a piece, you also learn every combination that piece can stand in. \emph{Puede ser} costs you nothing but the knowledge that Spanish speakers say it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puede ser}
  \item \emph{tal vez}, then \emph{puede ser}
  \item \emph{puede ser, no sé}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two pieces make \emph{puede ser}? (\emph{Poder} and \emph{ser}.) What happens to the \emph{o} of \emph{poder} under stress? (It breaks into \emph{ue}.) And which of the two answers so far concedes the most? (\emph{Puede ser}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[en efecto]{en efecto — a false friend with a warning on it}

\label{lesson:ES-C298-en-efecto}



\begin{quote}
What does \emph{tal vez} answer? (Maybe.) And which two pieces make \emph{puede ser}? (\emph{Poder} and \emph{ser}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item exacto — the answer this one stands next to.
  \item hacer — the doing that sits inside it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en e-FEC-to}, stress on the third beat. The \emph{c} before \emph{t} is a hard \emph{k}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{en efecto} — \textquotedblleft{}indeed,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}quite so.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Efecto} is Latin \textbf{effectus}: \emph{ex}, out, and \emph{facere}, to do — a thing carried out and finished. The same \emph{facere} you have been meeting inside \emph{hacer} since early on.

Now the warning. English \textbf{in effect} looks like the same phrase letter for letter, and it is not. \emph{In effect} means \textquotedblleft{}for practical purposes, though not formally\textquotedblright{} — it softens a claim. \emph{En efecto} hardens one: it says the thing someone just told you is so.

That is what makes it worth having. \emph{Exacto} agrees with a statement's precision. \emph{En efecto} agrees with the fact of it, and it is the one you will hear from somebody reading a document out loud and finding it says what you claimed.

Two words that look identical and pull in opposite directions is the most expensive kind of pair there is, because nothing warns you. This one is warned.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three answers, and the dial has turned. \emph{Tal vez} is a shrug, \emph{puede ser} is a concession, and \emph{en efecto} is agreement with the evidence in hand.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en efecto}
  \item \emph{exacto}, then \emph{en efecto}
  \item all three — \emph{tal vez}, \emph{puede ser}, \emph{en efecto}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two pieces are in \emph{effectus}? (\emph{Ex}, out, and \emph{facere}, to do.) Does \emph{en efecto} soften a claim or confirm one? (It confirms it.) And what does English \emph{in effect} do instead? (It softens.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sin duda]{sin duda — caught between two}

\label{lesson:ES-C298-sin-duda}



\begin{quote}
Three answers so far. Which is the shrug? (\emph{Tal vez}.) Which concedes? (\emph{Puede ser}.) And which confirms? (\emph{En efecto}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item seguro — the answer nearest to this one.
  \item en efecto — the answer just before it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sin DU-da}, weight on the second word. Both \emph{d} sounds are soft, the tongue barely touching. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sin duda} — \textquotedblleft{}no doubt,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}certainly.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Duda} comes from Latin \textbf{dubitare}, to waver, and \emph{dubitare} is built on \textbf{duo}, two. To doubt is to have two answers in front of you and no way to pick. That is a much better picture of the state than the English word gives you.

The same \emph{duo} is all over English. \textbf{Dubious}, obviously. \textbf{Double}, less obviously. And \textbf{doubt} itself, which came through French as \emph{doute} with no \emph{b} in it at all — the \emph{b} was inserted centuries later by scholars who wanted the Latin visible. English still writes it and still does not say it, which is exactly what Spanish does with the \emph{h} of \emph{horno}.

So \emph{sin duda} is \textquotedblleft{}without the two\textquotedblright{}: there is only one answer available, and this is it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four answers, and the dial is near its top. \emph{Sin duda} is stronger than \emph{en efecto}, because \emph{en efecto} agrees with what was said and \emph{sin duda} says there was never anything else to agree with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sin duda}
  \item \emph{seguro}, then \emph{sin duda}
  \item all four — \emph{tal vez}, \emph{puede ser}, \emph{en efecto}, \emph{sin duda}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What number is inside \emph{dubitare}? (Two.) Why does English write a \emph{b} in \emph{doubt}? (Scholars put it back to show the Latin.) And how strong is \emph{sin duda}? (Very — there is no second answer.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ni hablar]{ni hablar — not even that}

\label{lesson:ES-C298-ni-hablar}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: which answer is the shrug? (\emph{Tal vez}.) What is inside \emph{dubitare}? (\emph{Duo}, two.) And does \emph{en efecto} soften or confirm? (It confirms.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item ni — the first half, which you have had for a long time.
  \item hablar — the second.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ni a-BLAR}, and the \emph{h} is silent, so the two words run straight into each other. The \emph{r} at the end is one tap. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ni hablar} — \textquotedblleft{}out of the question,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}no chance.\textquotedblright{}

Again, nothing new. \emph{Ni} is \textquotedblleft{}nor, not even.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Hablar} is to speak. Together: \textquotedblleft{}not even speaking of it.\textquotedblright{} The refusal is not of the request — it is of the conversation about the request, which is a good deal more final.

English has the same manoeuvre in \textbf{out of the question} and in \textbf{don't even}. None of these say no to the thing; they say the thing is not eligible to be discussed, and that is why they close a subject where a plain no would only invite another round.

A caution. This is flat, and among strangers it can be rude. With friends it is ordinary, and often affectionate — the way English \emph{don't even} can be. Keep \emph{no, gracias} for people you have just met.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{tal vez}, \emph{puede ser}, \emph{en efecto}, \emph{sin duda}, \emph{ni hablar}.

Read in order they are a dial that runs from \textquotedblleft{}possibly\textquotedblright{} through \textquotedblleft{}yes, evidently\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}we are not discussing this.\textquotedblright{} Two of the five you built out of pieces you already owned, and one of them warned you about a word that looks like English and is not.

Answers are cheap to learn and dear to get wrong. Knowing which end of this dial you are standing on matters more than any single one of them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ni hablar}
  \item \emph{sin duda}, then \emph{ni hablar} — the two ends
  \item all five — \emph{tal vez}, \emph{puede ser}, \emph{en efecto}, \emph{sin duda}, \emph{ni hablar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ni hablar} refuse — the request, or the conversation? (The conversation.) Which two words is it made of? (\emph{Ni} and \emph{hablar}.) And which of the five would you use with somebody you had just met? (Not this one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
